reason: The numeric range is well supported: PopSci reports a measured maximum of 4.5 m/s (~10 mph) and PMC8663001 (Building and Environment, PIV study) reports a maximum instantaneous sneeze velocity of ~15.9 m/s (~35.6 mph), so 'about 10 to 35 miles an hour' is sound. The second sentence is not supported as written. PopSci attributes the long-standing exaggerated figure to William Firth Wells and states it as '100 meters per second, or 224 miles per hour' -- not 100 mph. The item has converted 100 m/s into '100 mph', which is a unit error that happens to land on a different (also-circulating) number, so the sentence reads as sourced when the source says something else. PopSci also dates Wells only as 'a mid-century researcher'; neither source says 1940s. Fix: state the debunked figure as ~100 m/s (about 224 mph), drop or source the '1940s' date, and note the figure was inferred from droplet sizes rather than measured. Confidence 'established' is otherwise defensible for the range if both sources are kept.

Citation resolves to a real and directly on-point review: Xu F, Rhodes EC, 'Oxygen uptake kinetics during exercise', Sports Medicine, 1999 (PMID 10368878), which describes VO2 rising exponentially to a steady state after exercise onset -- exactly the lag the item describes. The 'couple of minutes to catch up' framing is appropriately soft for a simplification, the 'feels harder than it should' framing is subjective but harmless, and there is no medical advice, body-composition framing, or unsafe instruction. Age-appropriate at 9.

Both citations are real but neither one addresses the claim at all -- this is the same-general-topic failure, not genuine support. PMC8663001 is 'Experimental measurements of airflow features and velocity distribution exhaled from sneeze and speech using particle image velocimetry' (Building and Environment): it measures sneeze airflow velocity for virus-transmission modelling and contains nothing about the eye-closing reflex. The PopSci piece 'FYI: How Forceful Is A Sneeze?' is likewise entirely about sneeze velocity and the Wells 224 mph myth, and does not mention eyes. So an item marked confidence 'established' currently has zero support for either of its two sentences, including the notable 'nobody has fully explained what the reflex is for'. The underlying claim appears true and is safe for a nine-year-old, so this is salvageable -- but it must be re-sourced to literature that actually covers the sneeze blink reflex before it can stay labelled 'established'. These two velocity citations look like they were copy-pasted from SF-FCT-000084.

Both URLs resolve, but the item is stated far more firmly than either source supports, and its own citation contradicts the 'established' label. (1) The Wikipedia endurance running hypothesis article explicitly presents this as a debated hypothesis and carries an 'Academic discourse' section recording that the proposed traits were called 'trivial' or 'incorrect' and that most remain untested; an item whose primary source labels the idea contested cannot be served as confidence 'established'. (2) Neither source says humans are 'the best long-distance runners in the animal kingdom'. Wikipedia makes the far narrower claim that 'no primates other than humans are capable of endurance running'; the UC Davis blog 'Humans are Born to Run' says only 'we may not be the best sprinters in the animal kingdom, we can run steadily for long distances, even in hot weather'. The superlative is the item's own invention, and it is disputed -- sled dogs, horses, camels and pronghorn are routinely cited as matching or beating humans over distance. (3) The mechanism sentence -- 'most animals can only cool down by panting, which they can't do while galloping' -- appears in neither source. The UC Davis page does not discuss panting while galloping at all, and Wikipedia explicitly does not. As stated it is also wrong: respiratory-locomotor coupling constrains a galloping quadruped's breathing, it does not make panting impossible, and horses and camels sweat substantially. Fix by reframing as the contested hypothesis it is ('one idea about why humans are unusually good at running in the heat'), setting confidence to 'contested' with the text saying so, dropping the superlative, and sourcing the panting claim to real physiology or cutting it.

The underlying fact holds (ROM peaks around 16:00, tracking core temperature) but the option text says 'Most people', which is an unsourced quantified claim under `simplified` — cite it (e.g. Reilly/Atkinson diurnal-variation work in Chronobiology International) or reword to 'tends to'. Guessability is also weak: option 2 ('flexibility is fixed') is eliminated by the stem's own wording, leaving a coin flip between options 0 and 3. Finally it duplicates SF-TRV-000306's mechanism — two items in this sample both teach 'X tracks body temperature, which peaks in the late afternoon'.

The explanation asserts one mechanism and rules out others with no source ('loops are broken by interruption more than by effort', 'It isn't about using up energy') — that is firmness beyond the evidence on a mental-health topic. It also never addresses distractor 3 (increased cerebral blood flow), which is partly true, so the reader is left with an unexplained wrong answer. Either hedge the mechanism ('one reason may be...') or cite the nature-walk rumination work. Consider adding a boundary line: a repeating thought that does not shift is worth telling an adult about, rather than implying a walk is the answer.

Correct (increased stroke volume, same cardiac output at fewer beats), and 'the heart is getting weaker' is a genuinely plausible naive distractor, which is what makes this the better of the two resting-heart-rate items. Note the duplicate: SF-TRV-000062 teaches the same fact with a copy-pasted explanation line; keep this one.

The keyed answer is wrong for the stem, and the explanation contradicts the key. Standard talk test: able to SING = light/easy; can talk but NOT sing = MODERATE; can't say more than a few words = vigorous. The stem asks about an 'easy pace' but keys the moderate band. The explanation then says 'singing means easy' — i.e. it states the correct taxonomy and disagrees with its own answer_index. Fix: either key the option to singing comfortably, or change the stem to 'a moderate pace'. Also drop the superlative 'the simplest way' from the stem. This one is currently teaching a child to treat moderate effort as their easy baseline.

Arithmetic checks out: 27 bones per hand and 26 per foot = 106 of about 206, i.e. just over half. The explanation pre-empts the common half-remembered version ('a quarter are in your feet') instead of restating the key, which is genuinely useful. Minor: 'More than half' is the only non-fraction phrasing, so it stands out slightly; consider 'About half' as a fourth fraction-style distractor.

Continuous bone remodelling is correct at every age, and the 'bone is finished material, like a shell' option is an elaborated real misconception rather than a bare dismissal. The explanation earns its place (fracture healing, load response, why growth stopping is not the same as remodelling stopping). Minor thematic overlap with SF-TRV-000089 on load response, but this item's payload is distinct.

Near-duplicate of SF-TRV-000032 in the same sample — same fact (resting heart rate falls with training), same mechanism, and a copy-pasted explanation sentence ('It's one of the few fitness changes you can watch happen — count for a minute now, and again in two months'). Keep SF-TRV-000032, which has the stronger distractor set, and cut or fully repurpose this one.

Correct and the explanation does the hard part — it explains WHY veins look blue (light scattering in skin) rather than just asserting that blood is always red. Distractors are the actual versions of the myth people hold. Safe and age-appropriate.

Anti-movement/stabilisation as the core's primary role is standard and correctly framed; all three distractors are partially true things the core also does, which is the right kind of distractor. Explanation teaches an application (carrying shopping one-handed) instead of restating.

Clean definitional item; the three distractors are the three qualities coordination is most often confused with (speed, strength, flexibility), and the catching-a-ball example does explanatory work. Age-appropriate at 9.

Guessable without knowing anything. The key is the only affirming, non-extreme option; the other three are an absolute ('Only running and jumping have ANY effect'), a flat either/or ('set by diet RATHER THAN movement') and a flat denial ('leaves the bone unchanged'). A reader who has learned that quiz absolutes are usually wrong scores this cold. Rewrite at least two distractors as plausible, non-absolute wrong beliefs (e.g. 'bone only responds to load while you are still growing'). Also overlaps SF-TRV-000049, which teaches the same load-response point in its explanation.

~90 minutes is the standard figure, and the explanation adds real content about the deep-sleep-early / REM-late distribution instead of restating. Distractor spread is sensible and nothing here is medical advice.

Slow-wave activity and memory consolidation in deep sleep are well established, and the contested glymphatic claim is correctly labelled AND stated as contested in the text — the 2013 Xie finding was directly challenged by Miao et al., Nature Neuroscience 2024, and remains disputed. This is the item in the sample that handles uncertainty properly. Minor: the key is the longest and most specific option; consider padding the distractors.

True and correctly framed as speed of availability, not as 'best' fuel. The explanation distinguishes all three distractors rather than restating the key, and there is no weight, body-composition or restriction framing anywhere in it.

Two of the three distractors are not plausible — 'Only if the food is served cold' is close to a joke, and 'Only in small amounts not worth counting' is a hedge nobody believes. The key is also the longest option and the only affirmative in a yes/no stem. Separately, 'A decent share of most people's daily fluid' is an unsourced quantified claim under `simplified`; the usual figure is roughly 20-30% from food and should be stated with a source or dropped.

True, age-appropriate, and the explanation earns its place with the haemoglobin fact rather than restating. Distractors are things a reader could genuinely misclassify, and the explanation is careful to say the three distractors are needed too, not worthless.

DOMS peaking at roughly 24-48 hours is correct and the 36-hour figure sits inside the accepted window. Distractors span the plausible range rather than being jokes, and the explanation adds a genuinely useful inference (the culprit is usually the session before last).

Answerable from the term itself: 'warm-up' rules out 'the hardest set' and 'done at the end' without any knowledge, leaving a two-way choice. Low information payload. Also 'Cheap insurance' implies injury prevention, which is exactly the over-firm framing the rubric names ('stretching prevents injury'); the defensible benefit is movement rehearsal and readiness, so say that and drop the insurance metaphor.

Both citations are real, on-topic and support part of the explanation, but not its two strongest assertions. PMC7076334 is 'The role of salivary contents and modern technologies in the remineralization of dental enamel: a narrative review' (F1000Research, 2020) and directly supports the acellular/no-regrowth point -- 'Being acellular, it cannot be automatically replaced or repaired if damaged' -- and the remineralization point: 'Saliva acts as a remineralizing agent and as a delivery vehicle of ions, like fluoride'. PMC10135549 is 'Analysis of Dental Enamel Remineralization: A Systematic Review of Technique Comparisons' (Bioengineering, 2023) and likewise covers remineralization. However: (a) neither source states that enamel is the hardest substance in the body or harder than bone -- which is the trivia question's actual answer and the explanation's opening claim -- so the item's central assertion is currently uncited even though it is true and uncontroversial; (b) 'which is most of what brushing is for' is not in either source and is stated too firmly -- brushing's primary mechanical role is biofilm/plaque disruption, with fluoride delivery as the key chemical benefit, so calling remineralization 'most of what brushing is for' overstates it. The hedge 'enamel that has started to soften' is correctly cautious and should be kept. Fix: add a source for the hardness claim and soften or cut the 'most of what brushing is for' clause. Question is otherwise safe and age-appropriate; distractor quality is adequate though 'the cartilage in your ears' is a weak option since cartilage is commonly known to be soft.

Mechanism is correct (sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction; denervated digits do not wrinkle). All four options are real candidate explanations, the osmosis distractor is the genuine popular misconception, and the explanation adds the evidence rather than restating the key.

Two defensible correct answers. Option 1 ('repetition at a set time trains the body to expect it') describes circadian/anticipatory learning, which is also a real reason a fixed time helps — and the explanation concedes this outright ('which is a different mechanism from your body learning a schedule'). If the item means to test context-cueing specifically, either narrow the stem to place only ('Why does a fixed PLACE help a habit stick?') or replace option 1 with something false.

Uneven-terrain stabiliser recruitment is a fair simplification, the explanation concedes that surface softness and gradient contribute too rather than pretending the distractors are worthless, and no option is a joke or a bare dismissal.

The teaching point is contradicted by the evidence. The explanation asserts that outdoor and indoor play are close on intensity ('the intensity and the duration are much closer than people assume'), but the literature is consistent the other way: children are roughly twice as active outdoors, and preschoolers need about 9.1 minutes indoors to accumulate a minute of MVPA versus 3.8 minutes outdoors. That makes option 3 ('more vigorous throughout') defensibly correct, so the item has two right answers and keys the wrong one. Options 0 and 1 are also arguably true. Cannot be fixed by swapping distractors — the premise needs rewriting, ideally into an item that teaches the intensity difference with a source.

Both citations resolve to real StatPearls chapters and directly support the claim. NBK546607 is 'Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Long Flexor Tendons and Sheaths', which states that 'Six long flexor muscles originate in the forearm but have tendon attachments in the hand'. NBK537229 is 'Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Muscles', which states directly that 'The intrinsic muscles of the hand provide the fine motor movements while the extrinsic muscles permit strength' -- supporting both halves of the explanation, including the force-versus-fine-control split. All four options are anatomically plausible to a non-expert, the correct option is not the longest or most specific, and no distractor is a joke or a bare dismissal. The 'make a fist and feel below your elbow' instruction is safe and self-verifying, and there is no body-composition, weight or medical framing. Age-appropriate at 9.

Eccentric loading as the cause of downhill-walking soreness is correct and well established. Distractors are all real lay explanations, the key is not the longest, and the explanation gives the mechanism plus the uphill contrast rather than restating.

'A disproportionate number of sporting records have fallen' in that window is a quantified empirical claim with no source under `simplified` — either cite it or cut the clause; the reaction-time point stands without it. Also a near-duplicate of SF-TRV-000006: same causal mechanism, same body-temperature-peaks-late-afternoon payload, same 'the effect is small' caveat. One of the two should go.
